clinicalPearls: Compression of the left common iliac vein between the overlying right common iliac artery and the underlying lumbar vertebra, typically at L5
Chronic pulsatile compression produces intraluminal venous spurs or webs and predisposes to left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis and left-sided venous hypertension
Classically presents in young to middle-aged women with left leg swelling, pain, varicosities, or an unprovoked left iliofemoral DVT
Should be suspected in left-sided iliofemoral DVT, especially when unprovoked or recurrent
Cross-sectional venography (CT or MR) demonstrates the compression, while intravascular ultrasound best quantifies the stenosis and any post-thrombotic change

Management of the acute thrombotic presentation combines anticoagulation with catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy in selected patients, followed by angioplasty and stenting of the compressed segment
Correcting the underlying compression with venous stenting reduces post-thrombotic morbidity and rethrombosis
reference.pathophysiology: May-Thurner syndrome arises from the anatomical position of the right common iliac artery crossing over and compressing the left common iliac vein against the fifth lumbar vertebra. Repetitive arterial pulsation and mechanical compression cause endothelial injury and the development of intraluminal venous spurs or webs, producing a fixed venous stenosis. This impairs venous outflow from the left leg, causing venous hypertension and greatly increasing the risk of left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis, which may present acutely or lead to chronic post-thrombotic sequelae.
additionalDifferentials: Deep vein thrombosis from other causes
Chronic venous insufficiency from superficial reflux
Extrinsic iliac vein compression by tumour or other mass
additionalInvestigations: Venous duplex ultrasound as an initial assessment, though it visualises the iliac segments poorly
CT or MR venography to demonstrate iliac vein compression and collaterals
Intravascular ultrasound to quantify the stenosis and guide stenting
Thrombophilia screen in unprovoked or recurrent thrombosis where appropriate
Assessment for post-thrombotic changes in chronic presentations
redFlags: Acute massive iliofemoral DVT with limb compromise (phlegmasia)
An extrinsic pelvic mass causing the compression
reference.prognosis: With recognition and treatment of the underlying compression by stenting, alongside thrombus removal and anticoagulation, outcomes are good with high stent patency; untreated compression predisposes to recurrent thrombosis and post-thrombotic syndrome.
pitfalls: Treating left iliofemoral DVT with anticoagulation alone and missing the underlying compression
Relying on duplex alone, which visualises the iliac veins poorly
Under-recognising the syndrome in young women with left leg swelling
Failing to use intravascular ultrasound and thereby underestimating the degree of stenosis
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
ESVS Clinical Practice Guidelines on Venous Disease
management: Anticoagulation for acute left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis
Catheter-directed thrombolysis or pharmacomechanical thrombectomy for extensive acute iliofemoral thrombosis in selected patients
Endovascular angioplasty and stenting of the compressed iliac vein segment as the definitive treatment of the underlying compression
Graduated compression therapy for limb swelling and post-thrombotic syndrome
Surveillance of stent patency with duplex imaging and continuation of antithrombotic therapy after stenting
Thrombophilia evaluation in unprovoked or recurrent thrombosis
Refer to vascular and interventional specialists for assessment and intervention
